title_original: «Le idee appartengono a tutti. Quindi a nessuno». Intervista a Viktor&Rolf
editorial_title_zh: “想法属于所有人。因此不属于任何人”。采访 Viktor&Rolf
editorial_excerpt_zh: 通过 Spectrum，这对荷兰组合在意大利的首场个展，10 Corso Como 重新审视了三十多年的探索。设计师 Viktor Horsting 与 Rolf Snoeren 谈论时尚中的作者性与权力。文章《“想法属于所有人。因此不属于任何人”。采访……》

article_text:
A 10 Corso Como, venti look di haute couture realizzati nell’arco di oltre trent’anni vengono messi in relazione senza seguire l’ordine del tempo. Viktor&Rolf. Spectrum , prima mostra personale in Italia dedicata a Viktor Horsting e Rolf Snoeren , costruisce il proprio percorso attraverso coppie, corrispondenze e variazioni, facendo dello specchio, del riflesso e della dualità una chiave per leggere una pratica che da oltre trent’anni attraversa moda, performance e cultura visiva. Curata da Alessio de’ Navasques , la mostra permette di osservare come alcuni nuclei della loro ricerca continuino a riemergere, trasformandosi nel tempo. Da qui il discorso si allarga naturalmente alla questione dell’autorialità, al rapporto tra opera e possesso, alla possibilità stessa di esercitare libertà critica dentro un sistema che tende ad assorbire e ridefinire i propri linguaggi. Con Viktor&Rolf la conversazione parte da Spectrum , ma arriva presto al nodo più difficile: chi possiede davvero un’idea una volta che è entrata nel mondo? Ne abbiamo parlato con Viktor&Rolf.

In Spectrum scegliete deliberatamente di allontanarvi dalla cronologia: invece di presentare il vostro lavoro come una progressione lineare, la mostra costruisce un sistema di corrispondenze, ritorni e trasformazioni. Guardando oggi opere create a molti anni di distanza, avete scoperto relazioni di cui non eravate consapevoli?

«Ogni stagione o collezione comincia con un senso di meraviglia, implica sperimentazione, una ricerca di novità e sorpresa. Allo stesso tempo, nel corso degli anni è diventato evidente che alcuni temi continuano ad affascinarci. Se per noi questo era evidente, è bello vedere questi punti tematici collegati da Alessio de’ Navasques e poter presentare questa curatela a 10 Corso Como».

La mostra si sviluppa attraverso coppie che non sono mai doppi esatti: affinità, variazioni e contrappunti. Eppure, nella storia dell’arte, lo specchio non si è limitato a confermare l’identità, spesso l’ha destabilizzata. Nel vostro lavoro, la dualità è ancora un principio di equilibrio oppure è diventata un dispositivo per produrre differenza?

«Lavoriamo molto attorno all’idea del doppio. Dell’avere due, o più, possibilità in una. Di opposti che, una volta plasmati o mostrati in condizioni differenti, creano un nuovo insieme. Ad esempio: gonfiato e sgonfiato; ben illuminato e oscurato; un fiore più una bomba uguale FB; oro tridimensionale e nero bidimensionale; immagini speculari realizzate in materiali contrastanti. In questo modo cerchiamo di esprimere punti di vista differenti, evitando di restare intrappolati in affermazioni assolute prive di sfumature».

Da tempo vi definite Fashion Artists . In origine, questa espressione metteva in discussione una separazione ancora piuttosto rigida tra moda e arte. Oggi il vostro lavoro appartiene alle collezioni di grandi musei ed è stato pienamente accolto dalle istituzioni culturali. Cosa accade a una definizione nata per destabilizzare le categorie quando quelle stesse categorie iniziano a legittimarla?

«La definizione è nata soprattutto per soddisfare le richieste dei media di avere un’etichetta. Chiamandoci Fashion Artists cercavamo di aggirare la domanda ricorrente su cosa fossimo e su cosa stessimo facendo. Per noi non contava allora e non conta oggi come veniamo chiamati. Il lavoro esiste nel mondo e, in qualche modo, risuona. A volte sommessamente, altre forte e chiaro».

La vostra prima mostra personale in Italia ha luogo a 10 Corso Como, uno spazio fondato sull’intersezione tra cultura, moda, design e commercio. La tensione tra opera e merce rimane ancora produttiva per voi oppure il sistema contemporaneo è ormai in grado di assorbire anche la critica che gli viene rivolta?

«Per noi le cose non sono così bianche o nere. Opere d’arte, merci, il sistema, la critica… possono tutti avere un ruolo nell’esprimere un’idea».

Viktor&Rolf è contemporaneamente il vostro nome, la vostra biografia creativa, un archivio, un linguaggio e una maison oggi di proprietà di OTB. Quale distinzione tracciate oggi tra essere Viktor&Rolf e possedere Viktor&Rolf?

«È curioso: Viktor e Rolf non possiedono più Viktor&Rolf. Bella domanda! Mi fa pensare a una delle nostre prime sfilate, nella quale una modella, Maggie Rizer, veniva vestita sul palco con nove strati consecutivi, come una bambola russa. Era concepita come un rituale che celebrava la creatività senza uno scopo commerciale diretto: una sfilata dedicata al piacere della bellezza senza poterla possedere. Questo era il pensiero. Poi quella collezione è stata acquistata da un museo. Dal momento che il museo non la concede in prestito, viene esposta molto raramente. In un certo senso, gli abiti sono scomparsi. La sfilata risale a prima di internet e ne rimangono poche immagini. Fu ripresa da una sola telecamera e per anni il filmato andò perduto. In un certo senso, quella sfilata non “esisteva” davvero. Quello che vogliamo dire è che quella sfilata vive soprattutto come idea, come racconto, come memoria, come momento della nostra carriera. Non come oggetti che possono essere posseduti. In quanto tale, è accessibile a tutti, appartiene a tutti. E dunque a nessuno. Anche se non siamo più i proprietari dei resti fisici del nostro lavoro, alla fine questo è relativamente poco importante. Perché il nostro compito è mandare idee nel mondo. Energia. Provengono dalle nostre menti, ma nemmeno noi le “possediamo”. Una volta entrate nel mondo appartengono a tutti, vale a dire a nessuno».

Vorrei tornare, infine, al titolo Spectrum . Uno spettro suggerisce una molteplicità di possibilità, ma anche zone che rimangono oltre i limiti della percezione. Quale parte di questo linguaggio vi rimane ancora opaca? Che cosa, della moda, continuate a non comprendere?

«Le dinamiche di potere.»

article_text:
Begun in 2023, the series “République” unfolds exclusively on the Paris square of the same name, extending a body of work on the notion of resistance that Bérangère Fromont has been developing for several years. The site is symbolic: in the collective imagination, it is the place of great popular gatherings, of revolts and revolutions. Yet the photographs, hosted by the Théâtre du Nord in Lille at the initiative of the Institut pour la photographie, do not openly speak of rebellion. Instead, a strange softness emanates from the monochromes and rich grays of the images hung on the theater’s white walls. They show bodies, those of young people (skaters in particular) who make the square their own, day after day. Bare-chested bodies, resting bodies, bodies that brush against and touch one another. The grain of the prints, delicately nuanced, becomes almost sensual. It sets portraits and architectural details in dialogue, like so many sculptural figures to contemplate.

A particular intention

“Bérangère Fromont carried out this project with a singular technique. She immersed herself in the square, going there every day at the end of the afternoon. She shot wide, with an 80mm lens and no zoom, then extracted details that she enlarged,” explains Florentine Bigeast, communications manager at the Institut. These elements, lifted from the wide frescoes she captures, are then printed with particular care, in piezography (using carbon ink) on a mulberry-fiber paper that is both thin and resilient. This refinement allows the subjects to seize the viewer’s gaze. Set against reworked black backgrounds, as if to underline their contours, they shift from anonymous figures to protagonists of a subtle narrative.

How resistance is expressed

“The photographer maintains that speaking about resistance through a project of apparent gentleness does not soften the message; on the contrary, it underscores it,” notes Florentine Bigeast. Rooted in a space heavy with symbolism (Place de la République evokes a well-known chapter of French history, but also recalls the many squares of the same name in other cities, which often mark the starting point of a demonstration), the project becomes compelling for what it leaves unsaid, for what it does not show. Here, skin is velvety, eyes are closed, shoulders relaxed. And yet “République” invites us to ask: where are the women in these pictures? What does their near-absence say about their place in public space? How is resistance expressed today? Can a peaceful revolt exist? How can these places be occupied outside moments of active protest?

At a time when high school students’ demonstrations, harshly repressed by the police, raise more than ever the question of young people’s role in a form of revolution, Bérangère Fromont’s exhibition reminds us that engagement also arises, sometimes, in the most ordinary actions.

“République” is on view at the Théâtre du Nord , Lille, through January 16, 2027.

Der immense Erfolg von Dörries drittem Spielfilm, der Beziehungskomödie „ Männer “ (1985), hat sich in der US-Filmbranche herumgesprochen: Martin Scorsese gratuliert der Regisseurin mit einem persönlichen Schreiben. Die Produktionsfirma Columbia Pictures bietet ihr einen Vertrag über fünf Filmprojekte. Doch auf Dick Cavetts Nachfrage, ob seine Information richtig ist, dass „Männer“ einer der erfolgreichsten Filme der deutschen Nachkriegsgeschichte sei, antwortet Doris Dörrie eher amüsiert: „I’m afraid so“, ja, leider sei das wohl so.

Denk ich an Deutschland. Über jüngere deutsche Komödien zu gesellschaftlichen und zwischenmenschlichen Konfliktfeldern

Auch mit zeitlichem Abstand ist „Männer“ die wohl schärfste und zugleich lustigste Sezierung westdeutscher Mentalitäten in den mittleren 1980er-Jahren. Heiner Lauterbach und Uwe Ochsenknecht spielen darin zwei Männer, die es sich recht unterschiedlich eingerichtet haben zwischen den nachklingenden Werten der 68er-Generation und den turbokapitalistischen Träumen des Yuppie-Zeitalters: Gegensätze, die letztlich eingeebnet werden beim verbindenden Streben nach einem höheren sexuellen Marktwert – seit jeher dem Grundantrieb jeder klassischen romantischen Komödie. Den Film bezeichnet die Regisseurin heute im Gespräch als ihre einzige „Straightforward Comedy“, obwohl ihr seitdem oft irrtümlich das Label angeheftet wird, eben jene Spielart der Beziehungskomödie, die sie mit „Männer“ popularisiert hat (und die bis heute die Erzählmuster vieler deutscher Mainstream-Lustspiele definiert), immer wieder aufs Neue zu variieren.

Bruch mit geradliniger Genrearbeit

Womöglich erklärt sich daraus das schon frühe Unbehagen, mit dem Doris Dörrie bereits in der „Dick Cavett Show“ auf den ersten großen Erfolg reagierte. In Zusammenarbeit mit Columbia dreht sie nach „Männer“ zunächst ihre einzige amerikanische Produktion: „ Ich und Er “ (1988), eine Verfilmung des gleichnamigen Romans von Alberto Moravia über einen New Yorker Architekten, dem sein mit ihm wortreich kommunizierender Penis das Liebes- und Beziehungsleben zu diktieren versucht. Gerade weil mit diesem Film wieder ein Rezept für Kassenerfolg aufzugehen scheint, bedeutet er für die Filmemacherin eine Zäsur, einen daran anschließenden, bis heute andauernden Bruch mit allzu geradliniger Genrearbeit. Was ihr Werk seitdem auszeichnet und im deutschsprachigen Kino in dieser Form singulär bleibt, ist eine Hinwendung zum komplex schillernden Tragikomischen, einem kunstfertig und gewandt erarbeiteten leichten Ton: „Ich mag es, wenn Dinge ambivalent und kompliziert sind und gleichzeitig eine gewisse Komik haben. Ich mag Filme nicht, die überhaupt keinen Sinn für Humor haben. Das finde ich immer schwierig.“

„ Keiner liebt mich “ (1994) und „ Bin ich schön? “ (1998) sind Höhepunkte eines deutschen Autorenkinos der 1990er-Jahre, das eigensinnig und kommerziell zugleich gedacht wird. Beziehungskiste und Trauerarbeit, Heiterkeit und Schwermut erweisen sich darin nie als Gegensätze, sind stets unterschiedlich gestimmte Tonalitäten, die bestens miteinander auskommen können. Die intrikat ineinander gewobenen Episoden von „Bin ich schön?“, gedreht mit einem Ensemble von 16 Hauptfiguren, besitzen dabei als zusammenlaufende Vignetten die präzise Pointiertheit und zugleich entspannte Nonchalance von Robert Altmans „ Short Cuts “ (1993). In ihnen zeigt sich das mühelos erscheinende erzählerische Geschick der Drehbuchschreiberin Doris Dörrie, welches sie ab 1987 auch jahrzehntelang als Autorin zahlreicher Kurzgeschichtensammlungen („ Für immer und ewig “, 1991), Romanen („ Das blaue Kleid “, 2002) und zuletzt entschieden autofiktional geprägten Texten („ Die Heldin reist “, 2022) beweist.

Neben der Noir-inspirierten Literaturverfilmung „ Happy Birthday, Türke “ (1991) ist „Keiner liebt mich“ eine von zwei Kinoregiearbeiten, die Dörrie zu dieser Zeit mit einer eigenen, kollektiv gegründeten Produktionsfirma, der Cobra Film, realisieren kann: „Wir waren zu sechst und hatten Kameramann, Regie, Geschäftsführung, einen Rechtsanwalt, einen Cutter und einen Produktionschef.“ Inmitten einer Filmförderlandschaft, die bis heute noch penibel zwischen konventionell zugeschnittenem Mainstream und übereifrig unterstellter Nische unterscheidet, entsteht so für einige Jahre ein unabhängiger, utopischer Freiraum, der sich erst wieder tragisch schließt, als einer der an Cobra Film maßgeblich Beteiligten, Dörries Ehemann, der großartige Kameramann Helge Weindler , bei Dreharbeiten im spanischen Almería verstirbt.

Ein neuer Look ab Ende der 1990er-Jahre

Weindlers kunstvoll arrangierte Kamerafahrten und Ideen für idiosynkratische Farbgebung (das frühe gemeinsame Meisterwerk „ Paradies “ beispielsweise ist ausschließlich mit unterschiedlichen Gelbfiltern vor der Linse gedreht) hatten bis dahin sehr maßgeblich den Look und die visuelle Ästhetik von Dörries Filmen geprägt. Ohne ihn weiterdrehen zu können ist für die Regisseurin erst wieder vorstellbar, als sie für sich eine andere, intime Methode des Filmemachens entdeckt. Ihr bis dahin unverstellt persönlichster Film, die gerade mal knapp einstündige Dokumentararbeit „ Augenblick “ (1998), entsteht mit radikal verkleinertem Filmteam und einer handlichen digitalen Kamera, die ihr der Regiekollege Werner Penzel schenkt: „Ich bekam durch dieses andere Format und diese andere Art zu arbeiten noch einmal eine große Freiheit. Das war schon immer mein Traum von Cinema Direct: die Kamera auf die Straße mitzunehmen. Das hat meine Arbeitsweise für die nächsten Jahrzehnte sehr stark bestimmt.“

Um die Jahrtausendwende ist die Arbeit mit digitalem Equipment eine Neuheit, deren Verheißungen so verlockend wie zunächst noch unbestimmt sind. Für Dörrie wird sie schnell zu einem verlässlichen Ideal, auch Spielfilmprojekte umstandsloser und dadurch freier realisieren zu können. „Für mich ist immer dieser Traum da: klein, beweglich und frei zu arbeiten. Und nicht durch große Logistik eingeengt zu werden“, sagt sie. „Am liebsten würde ich mit sechs Leuten und vier Schauspielern arbeiten.“

Betrachtet man heute Filme, die zu dieser Zeit im Mini-DV-Format gedreht wurden, seien es Danny Boyles Y2K-Horrorvision „ 28 Days Later “ oder Dominik Grafs impressionistischer Travelogue „ Der Felsen “ (beide 2002), betonen sie oftmals die expressiven, rohen Unzulänglichkeiten früher digitaler Kameras, deren Potenzial für bis dahin ungesehene, konfrontative Aufnahmen, die bald anschlussfähig werden sollten an die ungefilterten, rund um die Uhr fließenden Bilderströme des Internets. Doris Dörries erstem digital gedrehten Spielfilm, „ Erleuchtung garantiert “ (1999), ist gleichwohl die betont aggressive, experimentelle Ästhetik dieser Zeit vollkommen fremd. Auf Mini-DV zu arbeiten bedeutet für sie vielmehr, näher an Darstellern filmen zu können, den Geschichten eine zarte Vertraulichkeit einhauchen zu können: „Ich habe mir mit der Technik mehr Zeit mit den Schauspielern gekauft, wenn man so will. Ich wollte diese Freiheit mit den Schauspielern und diese Beweglichkeit haben. Diese Möglichkeit, dass die Realität mitspielen darf und dass man Dinge umschmeißt und ändert, weil sie sich entwickeln – das habe ich sonst nicht. Wenn ich mit so einem großen Apparat auftauche, kann ich die Richtung nicht mehr ändern, weil die Autos alle geparkt sind und nicht umgeparkt werden können und all diese Dinge. Und deshalb schwärme ich dafür.“

Faszination für Japan

Eine schwärmerische Intimität, die Begeisterungsfähigkeit und Neugier für menschliche Nähe verbinden seitdem viele Werke der Filmemacherin, auch wenn die Stoffe dabei kaum unterschiedlicher und diverser sein könnten: von der modernen Märchenbearbeitung „ Der Fischer und seine Frau “ (2004) hin zur frohgemuten Familienaufstellung „ Alles inklusive “ (2014) und der blutüberströmten Außenseiterromanze „ Glück “ (2012). Seit dem in Tokio gedrehten „ Erleuchtung garantiert “ wird auch zunehmend die Beschäftigung mit Japan für ihr Schaffen zentraler, eine Faszination, die bereits anderthalb Jahrzehnte zuvor begann: „Ich habe mit meinem allerersten Film Japan entdeckt. Ich war zu einem Festival eingeladen, zu ‚ Mitten ins Herz ‘, und bin dann dort hängen geblieben und herumgetrampt. Ich fand dieses irrsinnige Fremdsein und gleichzeitig diese große Vertrautheit so interessant.“

In Motiven dezidiert an Yasujijo Ozus „ Reise nach Tokio “ (1953) angelehnt, entsteht 2008 mit „ Kirschblüten – Hanami “ Dörries bis dato schönster und reichhaltigster Film. Ein von Elmar Wepper gespielter Rentner muss darin in der urbanen Fremde von Japan erst verloren gehen, um so ein tiefergehendes Verständnis für seine verstorbene Ehefrau ( Hannelore Elsner ) entwickeln zu können. Die rhapsodische Leichtigkeit der Geschichte verrät der Film dabei nicht an einen touristisch staunenden Blick auf die Schönheit des Unvertrauten: Eine Tanzszene vor dem prachtvoll aufragenden Anblick des Berges Fujiyama inszeniert die Regisseurin als einen fragilen, privaten Moment ohne jegliche auftrumpfende Grandiosität.

Wiederholte, lange Aufenthalte in Japan prägen die differenzierte Sicht Dörries auf das Land: „Es ist komisch in Japan, dass man sich dort auch so zu Hause fühlt, weil man so viel wiedererkennt“, resümiert sie. „Wir erkennen als Deutsche natürlich auch die komplette Zerstörung wieder. Viele Städte sehen aus wie Köln oder Hannover. Auch diese Besessenheit von Ordnung und Disziplin und diese Strenge und dieses Repressive – also der Versuch, alles, was wild und bunt und frei ist, sehr stark zu kontrollieren – ist sehr deutsch. Man findet so viel wieder und fühlt sich deshalb sehr schnell sehr vertraut oder fast zu Hause. Und gleichzeitig ist es total fremd.“ Von diesem unauflöslichen Widerspruch erzählt 2019 schließlich „ Kirschblüten & Dämonen “, ein Sequel zu „ Kirschblüten – Hanami “, das als vieldeutig, fernöstlich-bajuwarische Geistergeschichte zu den kühnsten und unergründlich faszinierendsten Filmen der Regisseurin gehört.

Freiheit jenseits aller Zuordnungen

Eine der Anleitungen zum autobiografischen Schreiben in Doris Dörries Buch „ Lesen, Schreiben, Atmen “ lautet: „Immer wieder über dasselbe schreiben, mit immer neuen Details.“ Worum ihre Filme kreisen und wozu sie immer wieder zurückkehren, ist in der cinephilen Rezeption gleichwohl bis heute verhältnismäßig wenig durchleuchtet worden, was angesichts eines rund fünf Jahrzehnte umfassenden Werks erstaunen muss. Dörrie bleibt eine sich nicht auf klare Genrearbeit festlegende Regisseurin, eine Arbeitsweise, die es bei der deutschen Filmkritik seit jeher schwer hat. „Eigentlich mag ich solche Labels gar nicht“, gibt sie zu bedenken. „Ich gehe selbst am liebsten in Filme, die keine Genrezuschreibung haben, bei denen ich für mich entdecken kann: Finde ich das jetzt sehr lustig, halblustig, sehr traurig oder traurig-komisch? Filme, die mir diese Freiheit geben und mich nicht durch ein Genre schon in meiner Wahrnehmung determinieren, finde ich am interessantesten.“ Jene Filme, die sich eine Freiheit jenseits all der Zuordnungen, die ihnen der Filmbetrieb aufdrängen möchte, erhalten, dreht auch heute niemand im deutschsprachigen Kino mit derart einnehmender Leichtigkeit und beständiger Überzeugung wie Doris Dörrie.

article_text:
Although Girls5eva was cut short after three seasons, Sara Bareilles still has some “Big P*ssy Energy” to work out with her inner Fledge Mulholland.

The 2x Grammy winner recently admitted she’s “still holding out” for a movie adaptation of the Peacock / Netflix series, which ran for three seasons from 2021 to 2024, noting that she and her co-stars would “do it in a heartbeat.”

“I would do that show until I was dead in the ground. I loved it so much,” she said on The Zach Sang Show . “They just stopped paying us to do it. I would do it for free—I maybe wouldn’t do it for free, but I would do it for very little.”

Related Stories

‘Girls5eva’ Canceled At Netflix & Will Not Have Season 4

Netflix Co-CEOs Address Executive Shakeup & Layoffs In Town Hall, Talk Up New CCO Peter Rice’s Experience Across Platforms — Including Streaming

Bareilles continued, “We wanted to tour. We wanted to do all kinds of things. I’m still holding out for a Sex and the City style movie, like a Girls5eva film. That feels finite, we could do it.”

Watch on Deadline

When asked if the rest of the cast would sign on, she said “100 percent,” adding, “They loved it. We loved it. We loved each other, and we loved doing that. I think we’d do it in a heartbeat.”

Created by Meredith Scardino, Girls5eva followed the four surviving members of the titular late ’90s/early aughts girl group as the reunite to make their comeback amid the stresses of being a woman of a certain age. Bareilles starred alongside Busy Philipps, Paula Pell, Renée Elise Goldsberry and Ashley Park.

article_text:
With something smart and pertinent to say about relationships between men and women, happiness and love, jealousy and longing and other matters of the heart, Wicker is the year’s most unexpected charmer.

A hit at Sundance where it was picked up by Black Bear , this wry film from writer-directors Alex Huston and Eleanor Wilson is sexy and satirically funny, but also oddly haunting as a truly twisted fable that says its never too late to become your own best version of Cinderella.

Case in point is The Fisherwoman (all the characters are identified by their profession or marital status), played to the hilt by Olivia Colman (who can do no wrong). In this storybook little village she is ostracized, acknowledged negatively by the town’s men for her fishy smell, insulted regularly when not being totally ignored. She’s sharp enough not to let it deter her, throwing off retorts like “lick my worm.”

How Olivia Colman Starrer ‘Wicker’ Went From Unpublished Short Story To A Big-Screen Feminist Romantasy

‘Wicker’ Red Carpet Premiere Photos: Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård, Elizabeth Debicki & More

Still we see she’s heartbreakingly lonely at home with little to keep her company, and so one day, after fate and the Bottle Washer’s wedding chooses her to be next in line, she wills it into truth and goes to the Basket Weaver ( Peter Dinklage ), a man with his own private loathing of the townspeople. She asks him point blank to make a wicker husband for her. Lo and behold he does in the strapping form of a bewickered Alexander Skarsgård (nicely tucked under the wicker facade), a beautifully crafted speciman who turns out to be a dream version of the perfect husband, one who professes he wants only what will make his new wife happy. Boy does he know how to do that!

Watch on Deadline

This unlikely pair have the hottest sex in town, practically destroying the furniture in the process. Suddenly like an aged Cinderella the Fisherwoman has hooked the big one and when word gets around, the locals are not happy about it, particularly Tailor’s Wife ( Elizabeth Debicki ), unfulfilled herself, who has a real problem with all of this and sets out to convince The Fisherwoman that her divine guy is actually unfaithful. The other townsfolk speculate on his prowess, his package, and why The Fisherwoman has lost all the dirt on her face and is now positively glowing.

In their deliciously entertaining film, Huston and Wilson mine this simple situation for all its worth, exploring how this event affects all the town’s marriages, the shortcomings of the men who take their wives for granted, the inherent unspoken misery of the women, the pervasive misogynist mentality, and the secrets and lies men and women keep from each other. When the male contingent wonder if the Basket Weaver can create the woman of their dreams things get really interesting.

Colman is incapable of playing any character with just one note, and here delivers another three-dimensional performance of a woman determined to change her life and find her happy place in it. Sarsgård touchingly underplays Wicker Husband and makes him undeniably more human, even more so than the other men who were born and not woven into being. Dinklage is perfect casting as the slightly duplicitous Basket Weaver, an artisan who has his own surprises in store. Debicki slips into the villain role with a nice subtlety that doesn’t hit us in the head with her evil plan to make The Fisherwoman regret ever conjuring up this dreamboat. The entire cast is in fact well chosen, including the underused Richard E. Grant as the doctor.

The craft of this little gem is exquisite including Lol Crawley’s gorgeous cinematography, Renato Cseh’s lovely production design that makes all this look like it was plucked right out of a Grimms’ Fairy Tale, and both the makeup and visual effects (Weta Workshop) teams which make wicker come wickedly to life in ways never before thought possible.

Producers are Ed Sinclair, Tom Carver, Colman, Justin Lothrop, Brent Stiefel, Brad Zimmerman, David Michod, Andrea Cornwell, Oliver Kassman, Tim Headington, Lia Buman, Ryan Heller and Michael Bloom.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Comedic multi-hyphenates Kate Berlant ( The Moment ) and John Early ( Maddie’s Secret ) are the latest additions to Naughty , the holiday comedy from Universal marking director Olivia Wilde’s follow-up to the lauded A24 chamber drama The Invite .

Character details are being kept in Santa’s sleigh. The duo joins a cast led by Jennifer Aniston and Peter Dinklage.

Related Stories

Kate Berlant Brings Laughs To A “Weird, Precarious” Moment – Comedy Means Business Podcast

‘Widow’s Bay’ Breakout Kate O’Flynn Joins Olivia Wilde Comedy ‘Naughty’ At Universal; Jamie Demetriou & Dexter Sol Ansell Also Set

This is just the latest of many collaborations for Early and Berlant, who as the latest guest on Deadline’s Comedy Means Business podcast, described Early as her “first real comedy friend” — a “sibling,” from whom she’s long been “inseparable.” The duo earned Emmy and Critics Choice Award nominations for their Peacock sketch special Would It Kill You to Laugh? and have also appeared together in Early’s recent feature directorial debut Maddie’s Secret , HBO Max’s Search Party , and much more.

Releasing in theaters on November 5, 2027, Naughty follows Mallory (Aniston), whose only hope of securing custody of her son from her gaslighting trash-bag ex is to find Santa Claus (Dinklage) and convince him to testify in her divorce hearing.

Watch on Deadline

Written by Cocaine Bear ‘s Jimmy Warden, the film also stars Chase Sui Wonders, Regina Hall, Ike Barinholtz and Samara Weaving. LuckyChap is producing alongside Wilde and Warden, with Executive Vice President of Production Development Sara Scott and Director of Production Development Jacqueline Garell overseeing the project for Universal.

Coming off the release of Parmesan — her second-ever comedy special, and first for HBO — Berlant’s recent credits include such films as The Moment and Wilde’s Don’t Worry Darling , as well as the hit series Nobody Wants This and The Bear .

Best known for starring alongside Alia Shawkat on Search Party , Early’s debut feature Maddie’s Secret , which he wrote and stars in, premiered as the opening night film in the Discovery section of the 2025 Toronto Film Festival before screening at the 2026 New Directors/New Films Festival and The Museum of Modern Art. Other recent credits include Coyote vs. Acme , the Tribeca indie comedy Never Change! , the final season of HBO’s The Comeback , and a role Off-Broadway in Wallace Shawn’s newest play What We Did Before Our Moth Days , directed by Andre Gregory.

Both Berlant and Early are repped by UTA and Rise Management. Berlant is also repped by Felker McGinnis & Ryan; Early by Jackoway Austen Tyerman.

article_text:
Art Review

Tacita Dean’s Truth in Materials

Instead of the slick stream of internet and AI imagery, the moving pictures projected onto a 31-foot-tall column are insistently material.

Tacita Dean: FILM (photo Monica Nouwens, courtesy the artist and Marian Goodman Gallery, New York/Paris, and Frith Street Gallery, London; all other photos Tara Anne Dalbow/

Hyperallergic )

LOS ANGELES — There is a certain irony to the formal correspondence between the endless scroll of a social media feed and a spool of 35mm photographic film. But what Tacita Dean’s monumental 2011 installation, FILM , makes clear is that the similarities end there. Instead of the slick, frictionless stream of homogeneous imagery circulating the internet, polished by filters and increasingly artificially generated, the moving pictures projected onto a 31-foot-tall column are insistently material: grainy, flickering, mottled by dust and interrupted by flashes of overexposure.

Sit for a moment in the pool of light reflected off the polished floor, head tilted upward, listening to the projector’s low whirring, and you’ll understand why the artist argued that transitioning from film to digital would mean changing artistic mediums completely. “It is not only emulsion versus pixels,” Dean wrote in an op-ed for the Guardian , “or light versus electronics but something deeper — something to do with poetry.” The simmering shots of cathedral windows and vine-ripe tomatoes feel sensuous, even vital.

Tacita Dean: FILM

First commissioned for Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall, the 11-minute silent film makes its United States debut in the similarly cavernous Theater Gallery at the Marciano Art Foundation in Los Angeles. The towering, vertical image, achieved by turning an anamorphic lens 90 degrees, looms like a colossal doorway in the dark. Sprocket holes that advance the celluloid through a projector border the composition, turning the screen into a massive film strip. Film is both Dean’s subject and her medium.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Omung Kumar ‘s ‘ Silaa ‘, starring Harshvardhan Rane , will release early next year.

Zee Studios has set a launch date of February 5, 2027, on the film, which stars Rane and Sadia Khateeb in a story billed as bringing together “intense romance, gripping mystery and high-octane action” set against the landscapes of Kashmir and Vietnam.

The storyline has broadly been kept secret, but it is known to center on the intense relationship between Virat (Rane) and Silaa (Khateeb) that takes a tragic and violent turn. You can see the first posters for the movie above.

Related Stories

Prime Video Adds Sony LIV To Indian Offer

The "Algorithm Breaking" 'Hunkkaar' Has Challenged Indian Audiences On The Limits Of Procedural TV - And Their Own Beliefs

“ Silaa has been one of the most challenging and exciting journeys for me as an actor,” said Rane in a statement to Deadline. “There is so much more to Virat than what meets the eye; he is a man driven by love, but when circumstances take an unexpected turn, he is pushed into a world where survival becomes just as important as finding the person he loves.”

Watch on Deadline

Kumar is directing the film, and produces alongside Himanshu Tiwari, Ajay Singh, Dhananjay Singh and Vanita Garud Kumar. Hemant Tiwari is co-producer. “With Silaa , we wanted to create a film that takes audiences on a roller-coaster ride, where romance, action, mystery and adventure come together in an unexpected way,” said Kumar.

“At its heart, the film is about love and the lengths a person can go to when everything they believe in is put to the test. We wanted the world of the film to feel expansive and visually striking, while ensuring that the emotions always remain at the centre of the story.”

Zee Studios made the pic along with Blue Lotus Pictures and Stark Entertainment.

title_original: Esposte a Ravenna le Pagine di Antonio Violetta, sculture-diario congelate nella materia
editorial_title_zh: 安东尼奥·维奥莱塔的《Pagine》在拉韦纳展出：凝固在物质中的日记雕塑
editorial_excerpt_zh: 直至2027年1月10日，萨贝艺术基金会空间正在举办名为“Pagine”的个人展览，展出雕塑家安东尼奥·维奥莱塔同名系列作品，由克劳迪奥·斯帕多尼策划。文章 安东尼奥·维奥莱塔的《Pagine》在拉韦纳展出：凝固在物质中的日记雕塑……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Pagine》不仅是一场展览，更是一段交织与回归的历史。首先，这是安东尼奥·维奥莱塔重回拉韦纳——这座这位卡拉布里亚雕塑家曾多次与之建立联系的城市，尤其是与拉韦纳市艺术博物馆（MAR）的合作。正是该博物馆携手拉韦纳美术学院以及博洛尼亚大学文化遗产系拉韦纳校区共同主办了本次展览，并出借了一件属于该馆馆藏的雕塑作品。", "links": [{"text": "Ravenna", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/tag/ravenna/"}, {"text": "MAR – Museo d’arte della Città di Ravenna", "url": "https://mar.ra.it/"}, {"text": "Accademia di Belle Arti di Ravenna", "url": "https://www.abaravenna.it/"}, {"text": "Dipartimento di Beni Culturali dell’Università di Bologna – Campus di Ravenna", "url": "https://beniculturali.unibo.it/it/index.html"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/1-Antonio-Violetta-Pagine-1985-terracotta-antirombo-luce-ai-vapori-di-sodio-100-x-210-cm.-Ph.-G.-Piacentini-1024x892.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "安东尼奥·维奥莱塔，《Pagine》，1985年，陶土、防石击涂料、钠蒸气灯，100 x 210 cm。摄影：G. Piacentini", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这一活动还标志着拉韦纳市艺术博物馆（MAR）与萨贝艺术基金会（Fondazione Sabe per l’arte）的首次合作。该基金会成立于2021年，致力于雕塑和当代艺术的发展。展览策展人克劳迪奥·斯帕多尼本人正是连接这两家机构的桥梁人物。这位师从弗朗切斯科·阿尔坎杰利的著名艺术史学家曾于2002年至2014年担任MAR馆长，现为基金会科学委员会成员；该基金会由诺贝托·贝齐和艺术家米雷拉·萨卢佐共同主持，艺术总监为评论家兼学者帕斯夸莱·法梅利。", "links": [{"text": "MAR", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/tag/mar-museo-darte-della-citta-di-ravenna/"}, {"text": "Fondazione Sabe per l’arte", "url": "https://www.sabeperlarte.org/"}, {"text": "Claudio Spadoni", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/tag/claudio-spadoni/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Antonio-Violetta-Pagine-installation-view-della-mostra-presso-Fondazione-Sabe-per-larte-di-Ravenna.-Ph.-Daniele-Casadio-18-1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "安东尼奥·维奥莱塔，《Pagine》，拉韦纳萨贝艺术基金会展览现场。摄影：Daniele Casadio", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正是曾担任多家国家级重要艺术机构委员会成员的斯帕多尼，将安东尼奥·维奥莱塔引荐至1986年第42届威尼斯双年展。这段深厚的友谊拉开了序幕，而本次展览正是又一次的印证。在与艺术家共同挑选的展品中，还包括两件属于《Lunarie》系列的作品，该系列正是于1986年在双年展上首次亮相。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/3-Antonio-Violetta-Lunarie-1986-terracotta-grafite-ferro-e-luce-ai-vapori-di-sodio-150-x-150-x-40-cm.-Ph.-G.-Artese-1020x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "安东尼奥·维奥莱塔，《Lunarie》，1986年，陶土、石墨、铁及钠蒸气灯，150 x 150 x 40 cm。摄影：G. Artese", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为展览同名作品系列的《Pagine》则于1984年展出，它标志着安东尼奥·维奥莱塔职业生涯中的一个关键节点，凝练了贯穿这位雕塑家整个创作生涯的一些主题，最早可追溯至20世纪70年代的早期个展。事实上，早期的《Carte catramate》就已经探讨了那个将二维与三维分隔开来的边缘而不确定的空间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Antonio-Violetta-Pagine-installation-view-della-mostra-presso-Fondazione-Sabe-per-larte-di-Ravenna.-Ph.-Daniele-Casadio-15-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "安东尼奥·维奥莱塔，《Pagine》，拉韦纳萨贝艺术基金会展览现场。摄影：Daniele Casadio", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "维奥莱塔本人的教育背景便处于这两种现实之间：这位最近被授予旨在表彰博洛尼亚市具有代表性艺术人物的沃尔波尼奖章的艺术家，最初是在博洛尼亚美术学院学习绘画而非雕塑，后来才转向三维创作，而这日后成为了他艺术探索的核心。作品所体现的时刻同样具有边缘性：它们虽然坚固紧凑，却带有一种童真般的延展性与未完成感，看起来几乎像是依然充满生机、处于演变中的团块。就好像人们依然可以对它们进行干预，但只是选择不去这样做。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/4-Antonio-Violetta-Infiniti-1987-terracotta-e-grafite-h-100-cm-Courtesy-MAR-–-Museo-d’Arte-della-Città-di-Ravenna-1024x940.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "安东尼奥·维奥莱塔，《Infiniti》，1987年，陶土和石墨，高100 cm，鸣谢拉韦纳市艺术博物馆（MAR）", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "雕塑的陈列方式也强调了这一点：它们没有被当作真理装裱起来，而是作为一种假设放置在地面上。这些带有发光闪现的单色形体并非既成事实，它们依然存在于我们这个可改变的、暂时的世界中。处于纸张的二维性与转化为体积质感之间，《Pagine》构成了动作的记录场，是一页原始而直观的日记，捕捉了转瞬即逝的情感的痕迹。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/6-Antonio-Violetta-Pagina-2025-terracotta-e-grafite-h-101-cm.-Ph.-A.-Violetta-690x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "安东尼奥·维奥莱塔，《Pagina》，2025年，陶土和石墨，高101 cm。摄影：A. Violetta", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "黏土上的沟槽固定了思维的轨迹，创造出其创作瞬间的感官地图。对远古手工艺的呼应也通过材料的选择——陶土和石墨——得以凸显，甚至在展厅的历史中也隐约可见：这里在19世纪曾是一家木工厂，后来成为印刷厂，在成为艺术画廊之前，最终变成了基金会举办展览的大厅。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在这个宽敞的空间里，《Pagine》傲然挺立，它们依然具有延展性，正处于物质与形式之间充满活力的蜕变之中，宛如一尊尊黏土制成的达芙妮，在化为月桂树的前一刻。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Pagine, oltre che una mostra, è una storia di intrecci e di ritorni. In primis , il ritorno di Antonio Violetta a Ravenna , città con cui lo scultore calabrese ha intessuto rapporti in più occasioni, in particolar modo col MAR – Museo d’arte della Città di Ravenna . È proprio quest’ultimo, insieme all’ Accademia di Belle Arti di Ravenna e al Dipartimento di Beni Culturali dell’Università di Bologna – Campus di Ravenna , a patrocinare la mostra, prestando oltretutto un’opera dello scultore appartenente alle collezioni del museo.", "links": [{"text": "Ravenna", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/tag/ravenna/"}, {"text": "MAR – Museo d’arte della Città di Ravenna", "url": "https://mar.ra.it/"}, {"text": "Accademia di Belle Arti di Ravenna", "url": "https://www.abaravenna.it/"}, {"text": "Dipartimento di Beni Culturali dell’Università di Bologna – Campus di Ravenna", "url": "https://beniculturali.unibo.it/it/index.html"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/1-Antonio-Violetta-Pagine-1985-terracotta-antirombo-luce-ai-vapori-di-sodio-100-x-210-cm.-Ph.-G.-Piacentini-1024x892.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Antonio Violetta, Pagine, 1985, terracotta, antirombo, luce ai vapori di sodio, 100 x 210 cm. Ph. G. Piacentini", "credit": "Exibart"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "L’evento sancisce inoltre la prima collaborazione tra il MAR e la Fondazione Sabe per l’arte , nata nel 2021 con la vocazione per la scultura e l’arte contemporanea in genere. Lo stesso curatore della mostra, Claudio Spadoni , è una figura-ponte tra le due istituzioni. Il celebre storico dell’arte allievo di Francesco Arcangeli è infatti stato direttore del MAR dal 2002 al 2014 e fa ora parte del comitato scientifico della Fondazione; quest’ultima è presieduta da Norberto Bezzi e dall’artista Mirella Saluzzo e ha come direttore artistico il critico e studioso Pasquale Fameli .", "links": [{"text": "MAR", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/tag/mar-museo-darte-della-citta-di-ravenna/"}, {"text": "Fondazione Sabe per l’arte", "url": "https://www.sabeperlarte.org/"}, {"text": "Claudio Spadoni", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/tag/claudio-spadoni/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Antonio-Violetta-Pagine-installation-view-della-mostra-presso-Fondazione-Sabe-per-larte-di-Ravenna.-Ph.-Daniele-Casadio-18-1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Antonio Violetta, Pagine, installation view della mostra presso Fondazione Sabe per l’arte di Ravenna. Ph. Daniele Casadio", "credit": "Exibart"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Fu lo stesso Spadoni, che è stato membro delle commissioni di alcune tra le più importanti istituzioni artistiche nazionali, a introdurre Antonio Violetta alla XLII Biennale di Venezia del 1986, agli albori di un lungo rapporto di amicizia che vede nella mostra un’ennesima riconferma. Tra i pezzi esposti, selezionati insieme all’artista, sono presenti anche due opere appartenenti alla serie Lunarie , presentata proprio nel 1986 in occasione della Biennale."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/3-Antonio-Violetta-Lunarie-1986-terracotta-grafite-ferro-e-luce-ai-vapori-di-sodio-150-x-150-x-40-cm.-Ph.-G.-Artese-1020x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Antonio Violetta, Lunarie, 1986, terracotta, grafite, ferro e luce ai vapori di sodio, 150 x 150 x 40 cm. Ph. G. Artese", "credit": "Exibart"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Pagine , il ciclo di opere da cui la mostra prende il titolo, viene invece presentata nel 1984 e segna un punto nodale nella carriera di Antonio Violetta, condensando alcuni dei temi che attraversano l’intera opera dello scultore, sin dalle prime personali degli anni Settanta. Già le Carte catramate , infatti, esplorano quel luogo liminale e incerto che separa la seconda e la terza dimensione."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Antonio-Violetta-Pagine-installation-view-della-mostra-presso-Fondazione-Sabe-per-larte-di-Ravenna.-Ph.-Daniele-Casadio-15-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Antonio Violetta, Pagine, installation view della mostra presso Fondazione Sabe per l’arte di Ravenna. article_text:
Pagine, oltre che una mostra, è una storia di intrecci e di ritorni. In primis , il ritorno di Antonio Violetta a Ravenna , città con cui lo scultore calabrese ha intessuto rapporti in più occasioni, in particolar modo col MAR – Museo d’arte della Città di Ravenna . È proprio quest’ultimo, insieme all’ Accademia di Belle Arti di Ravenna e al Dipartimento di Beni Culturali dell’Università di Bologna – Campus di Ravenna , a patrocinare la mostra, prestando oltretutto un’opera dello scultore appartenente alle collezioni del museo.

L’evento sancisce inoltre la prima collaborazione tra il MAR e la Fondazione Sabe per l’arte , nata nel 2021 con la vocazione per la scultura e l’arte contemporanea in genere. Lo stesso curatore della mostra, Claudio Spadoni , è una figura-ponte tra le due istituzioni. Il celebre storico dell’arte allievo di Francesco Arcangeli è infatti stato direttore del MAR dal 2002 al 2014 e fa ora parte del comitato scientifico della Fondazione; quest’ultima è presieduta da Norberto Bezzi e dall’artista Mirella Saluzzo e ha come direttore artistico il critico e studioso Pasquale Fameli .

Fu lo stesso Spadoni, che è stato membro delle commissioni di alcune tra le più importanti istituzioni artistiche nazionali, a introdurre Antonio Violetta alla XLII Biennale di Venezia del 1986, agli albori di un lungo rapporto di amicizia che vede nella mostra un’ennesima riconferma. Tra i pezzi esposti, selezionati insieme all’artista, sono presenti anche due opere appartenenti alla serie Lunarie , presentata proprio nel 1986 in occasione della Biennale.

Pagine , il ciclo di opere da cui la mostra prende il titolo, viene invece presentata nel 1984 e segna un punto nodale nella carriera di Antonio Violetta, condensando alcuni dei temi che attraversano l’intera opera dello scultore, sin dalle prime personali degli anni Settanta. Già le Carte catramate , infatti, esplorano quel luogo liminale e incerto che separa la seconda e la terza dimensione.

La formazione stessa di Violetta si trova in bilico tra queste due realtà: l’artista, recentemente insignito della Targa Volponi per le figure artistiche particolarmente rappresentative della città di Bologna, studia infatti presso l’Accademia di Belle Arti di Bologna come pittore, non come scultore, approdando solo successivamente alla tridimensionalità, che sarà poi il fulcro fondamentale della sua ricerca artistica. Liminale è anche l’istante incarnato dalle opere che, pur essendo solide e compatte, portano in sé un senso fanciullesco di malleabilità, di non finito, e sembrano quasi delle masse ancora vive e in divenire. È come se si potesse ancora intervenire su di esse, ma semplicemente si scegliesse di non farlo.

A sottolinearlo è anche la modalità espositiva delle sculture: non incorniciate come verità, ma posate a terra come ipotesi. Questi corpi monocromi con incursioni luminescenti non sono dei fatti compiuti, giacciono ancora nel nostro mondo, quello del modificabile, del temporaneo. A metà tra la bidimensionalità del foglio e il diventare volume e consistenza, le Pagine costituiscono un campo di registrazione del gesto, una pagina di diario primordiale e istintiva che cattura su di sé i segni di un’emozione fugace.

I solchi sull’argilla fissano le vie del pensiero, creando una mappa sensoriale del momento della loro stessa creazione. Il richiamo a un’artigianalità ancestrale è segnato anche dalla scelta dei materiali, terracotta e grafite, e aleggia perfino nella storia dello spazio espositivo, che fu falegnameria nell’Ottocento e poi tipografia, prima di diventare galleria d’arte e infine salone per le mostre organizzate dalla Fondazione.

In questo ampio spazio campeggiano le Pagine , ancora duttili e colte nel mezzo della vibrante metamorfosi tra materia e forma, quasi delle Dafne di creta, un istante prima di diventare alloro.

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Walker Evans was given a major exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art in 1971. That same year, Evans and his friend Leslie George Katz, publisher of Eakins Press, collaborated on an extensive interview. At this retrospective moment of his life, Evans wanted to record his thoughts on photography, his work, and the influences on him. He wanted to codify his legacy. In addition to the interview, Evans selected and commented on eight photographs that spanned the arc of his life’s work. While the interview and the photographs appeared at the time in Art in America , the project didn’t see book form until 1995, when Eakins Press published Walker Evans: Incognito . Charles Baudelaire, one of Evans’s greatest influences, wrote, “The observer is a prince enjoying his incognito wherever he goes.” This suggests that the observer, like a prince traveling in disguise, has a privileged position: They can move through the world anonymously, seeing everything while remaining unseen themselves."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The picture of a gutter was the most recent and least-known photograph in Evans’s selection. It is from 40 Studies of Street Debris, Manhole Covers, and Trash Bins, New York City (ca. 1968). Here is Evans’s accompanying text:"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While removed from nature, this picture of a gutter is in a sense very human. It is Baudelairean. I wish Baudelaire was alive to see it. The secret of photography is, the camera takes on the character and the personality of the handler. The mind works on the machine."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When Evans wrote “Baudelairean,” he was referring to this paragraph, describing a chiffonnier , a ragpicker, from Baudelaire’s essay “On Wine and Hashish”:"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Here is a man whose task it is to pick up all the rubbish produced on one day in the capital. All that the great city has thrown out, all that it has lost, all that it has disdained, all that it has broken, he catalogues and collects. He consults the archives of debauchery, works through the lumber-room of rubbish. He sorts things out and makes a selection, chooses astutely; like a miser, he collects the muck which, once more digested by the Gods of Commerce, will become objects of utility or pleasure."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/2026_Aperture264_1600x900_Fan_gray-copy.jpg", "alt": "Aperture Magazine Subscription", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Aperture Magazine Subscription"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Like the ragpicker, a photographer “catalogues and collects”—a photographer “sorts things out” and “chooses astutely.” Here, Evans looks at a city’s debris, a most common and lowly subject, and in the image he offers a taste of his mind. As Evans elaborated in the interview, “The mind works on the machine—through it, rather.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Writing now in my late seventies, I know that a time may come when a person reviews their past actions and experiences and recontextualizes them in the light of the perspective of a lifetime. In his interview with Katz, Evans looked back on the experience of his hot streak in the 1930s. He called the experience “a very exciting, heady thing,” adding that “it goes like magic” and “I use the word transcendent .” Evans is describing what I call a gift state. Many artists and writers have the feeling, for a period of time, of something taking over, of something working through them. Evans was now connecting the transcendence of his experience making the work with the transcendence conveyed by the images. They were imprinted with a quality of his mind."}, {"type": "quote", "text": "Focus is the nexus that connects the photograph, the world, and the mind. It is the door to the passage from the surface to the interior."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The only time I had the opportunity to hear Evans speak was at a lecture he gave at the Museum of Modern Art in the early 1970s. He showed Corrugated Tin Façade (1936)—a deadpan photograph of a dilapidated contractor’s office in Alabama, sunlight shimmering off the corrugation—and, by my recollection, called it a “transcendent document.” I knew that he had previously described “documentary style” as having the qualities of “severity, rigor, simplicity, clarity . . . without artistic pretension.” I was not expecting him to describe his work as transcendent. He was now indicating that below the surface of a “document” could lie an interior depth. He chose Matisse’s quote “L’exactitude n’est pas la vérité” (Exactitude is not truth) as the epigraph for his book Message from the Interior (1966). He is saying not to mistake the surface exactitude of documentary style for truth, but to look beneath the surface. Truth may be buried in its interior, the message from the interior. Truth can reside beneath the surface of the mundane, the quotidian. This recalls an Arab maxim, “The apparent is the bridge to the real.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "An Evans photograph in which I feel this depth, this undercurrent, an image that moves me most deeply, is Breakfast Room at Belle Grove Plantation , from March 1935. In an early act of urban exploration, Evans, accompanied by his future wife Jane Ninas and her friend Christine Fairchild, broke into the Belle Grove mansion. They shared a picnic breakfast in this space he would later call the “breakfast room.” Before making the photograph, Evans arranged the shutters in the center of the picture, allowing just a crack of light to seep through."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Belle Grove Plantation in White Castle, Louisiana, was built by the sugar planter John Andrews in 1857. The seventy-five-room Greek Revival mansion was one of the largest residential buildings in the American South during the antebellum period. Belle Grove exemplified the grand architectural ambitions of Louisiana’s sugar aristocracy and stood as a testament to the economic power generated by the brutal system of enslaved labor that perpetuated this culture. Without enslaved labor, the plantation could not be sustained. It changed hands several times after the Civil War and was eventually abandoned. By the early twentieth century, the mansion had fallen into serious disrepair."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/264MAG021_Notebook_Shore_HR.jpg", "alt": "Breakfast Room at Belle Grove Plantation, White Chapel, Louisiana. March 1935. Gelatin silver print, 6 15/16 x 8 9/16", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/264MAG022_Notebook_Shore_HR.jpg", "alt": "The Fall of the Giants. c. 1532-34.", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When I see the decaying Corinthian columns in the breakfast room, I think of Giulio Romano’s Sala dei Giganti (Hall of the Giants) in the Palazzo Te. Here the giants are trying in vain to hold up crumbling columns, massive columns tilting and breaking apart, the classical world disintegrating around them, as Zeus and the gods crush the giants for their hubris."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Look at the photograph Breakfast Room at Belle Grove Plantation . Slowly, deliberately, move your attention, your focus, along the side walls to the columns, then to the floor of the small vestibule, and then to the shutters. Notice the depth of space from the columns, across the vestibule, to the shutters. Do you have a sensation of your eyes changing focus? Do you sense Evans’s experience? Do you have a taste of Evans’s mind?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Focus is the nexus that connects the photograph, the world, and the mind. It is the door to the passage from the surface to the interior. It is a way of connecting with the mind that works through the machine."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This article originally appeared in Aperture No. 264, “Stop Time,” guest edited by Hiroshi Sugimoto, under the column Notebook."}]

Walker Evans was given a major exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art in 1971. That same year, Evans and his friend Leslie George Katz, publisher of Eakins Press, collaborated on an extensive interview. At this retrospective moment of his life, Evans wanted to record his thoughts on photography, his work, and the influences on him. He wanted to codify his legacy. In addition to the interview, Evans selected and commented on eight photographs that spanned the arc of his life’s work. While the interview and the photographs appeared at the time in Art in America , the project didn’t see book form until 1995, when Eakins Press published Walker Evans: Incognito . Charles Baudelaire, one of Evans’s greatest influences, wrote, “The observer is a prince enjoying his incognito wherever he goes.” This suggests that the observer, like a prince traveling in disguise, has a privileged position: They can move through the world anonymously, seeing everything while remaining unseen themselves.

The picture of a gutter was the most recent and least-known photograph in Evans’s selection. It is from 40 Studies of Street Debris, Manhole Covers, and Trash Bins, New York City (ca. 1968). Here is Evans’s accompanying text:

While removed from nature, this picture of a gutter is in a sense very human. It is Baudelairean. I wish Baudelaire was alive to see it. The secret of photography is, the camera takes on the character and the personality of the handler. The mind works on the machine.

When Evans wrote “Baudelairean,” he was referring to this paragraph, describing a chiffonnier , a ragpicker, from Baudelaire’s essay “On Wine and Hashish”:

Here is a man whose task it is to pick up all the rubbish produced on one day in the capital. All that the great city has thrown out, all that it has lost, all that it has disdained, all that it has broken, he catalogues and collects. He consults the archives of debauchery, works through the lumber-room of rubbish. He sorts things out and makes a selection, chooses astutely; like a miser, he collects the muck which, once more digested by the Gods of Commerce, will become objects of utility or pleasure.

Aperture Magazine Subscription

Like the ragpicker, a photographer “catalogues and collects”—a photographer “sorts things out” and “chooses astutely.” Here, Evans looks at a city’s debris, a most common and lowly subject, and in the image he offers a taste of his mind. As Evans elaborated in the interview, “The mind works on the machine—through it, rather.”

Writing now in my late seventies, I know that a time may come when a person reviews their past actions and experiences and recontextualizes them in the light of the perspective of a lifetime. In his interview with Katz, Evans looked back on the experience of his hot streak in the 1930s. He called the experience “a very exciting, heady thing,” adding that “it goes like magic” and “I use the word transcendent .” Evans is describing what I call a gift state. Many artists and writers have the feeling, for a period of time, of something taking over, of something working through them. Evans was now connecting the transcendence of his experience making the work with the transcendence conveyed by the images. They were imprinted with a quality of his mind.

Focus is the nexus that connects the photograph, the world, and the mind. It is the door to the passage from the surface to the interior.

The only time I had the opportunity to hear Evans speak was at a lecture he gave at the Museum of Modern Art in the early 1970s. He showed Corrugated Tin Façade (1936)—a deadpan photograph of a dilapidated contractor’s office in Alabama, sunlight shimmering off the corrugation—and, by my recollection, called it a “transcendent document.” I knew that he had previously described “documentary style” as having the qualities of “severity, rigor, simplicity, clarity . . . without artistic pretension.” I was not expecting him to describe his work as transcendent. He was now indicating that below the surface of a “document” could lie an interior depth. He chose Matisse’s quote “L’exactitude n’est pas la vérité” (Exactitude is not truth) as the epigraph for his book Message from the Interior (1966). He is saying not to mistake the surface exactitude of documentary style for truth, but to look beneath the surface. Truth may be buried in its interior, the message from the interior. Truth can reside beneath the surface of the mundane, the quotidian. This recalls an Arab maxim, “The apparent is the bridge to the real.”

An Evans photograph in which I feel this depth, this undercurrent, an image that moves me most deeply, is Breakfast Room at Belle Grove Plantation , from March 1935. In an early act of urban exploration, Evans, accompanied by his future wife Jane Ninas and her friend Christine Fairchild, broke into the Belle Grove mansion. They shared a picnic breakfast in this space he would later call the “breakfast room.” Before making the photograph, Evans arranged the shutters in the center of the picture, allowing just a crack of light to seep through.

The Belle Grove Plantation in White Castle, Louisiana, was built by the sugar planter John Andrews in 1857. The seventy-five-room Greek Revival mansion was one of the largest residential buildings in the American South during the antebellum period. Belle Grove exemplified the grand architectural ambitions of Louisiana’s sugar aristocracy and stood as a testament to the economic power generated by the brutal system of enslaved labor that perpetuated this culture. Without enslaved labor, the plantation could not be sustained. It changed hands several times after the Civil War and was eventually abandoned. By the early twentieth century, the mansion had fallen into serious disrepair.

When I see the decaying Corinthian columns in the breakfast room, I think of Giulio Romano’s Sala dei Giganti (Hall of the Giants) in the Palazzo Te. Here the giants are trying in vain to hold up crumbling columns, massive columns tilting and breaking apart, the classical world disintegrating around them, as Zeus and the gods crush the giants for their hubris.

Look at the photograph Breakfast Room at Belle Grove Plantation . Slowly, deliberately, move your attention, your focus, along the side walls to the columns, then to the floor of the small vestibule, and then to the shutters. Notice the depth of space from the columns, across the vestibule, to the shutters. Do you have a sensation of your eyes changing focus? Do you sense Evans’s experience? Do you have a taste of Evans’s mind?

Focus is the nexus that connects the photograph, the world, and the mind. It is the door to the passage from the surface to the interior. It is a way of connecting with the mind that works through the machine.

This article originally appeared in Aperture No. 264, “Stop Time,” guest edited by Hiroshi Sugimoto, under the column Notebook.

article_text:
Satiating your hunger for abstraction will take you all over New York this fall, from the Upper East Side to Chelsea to Tribeca. The works on view in the city’s galleries range from decades-old works to fresh interventions into ongoing series. Each show offers one artist’s singular approach to a never-ending investigation into how to create and derive meaning from non-representational painting and sculpture. By visiting these shows, you’ll see how artists from different generations have employed gesture, mark making, color, and form in different ways—all of which are feasts for the eyes.

For even more abstraction, be sure to check out MoMA PS1’s “Hard Art” exhibition, which looks at the legacy of abstract art by Black artists. The show includes work by three of the artists highlighted below— Mildred Thompson, Mary Lovelace O’Neal, and Virginia Jaramillo—all of whom have gallery shows on view this month.

Virginia Jaramillo at Hales Image Credit: Courtesy Hales For the past seven decades, Virginia Jaramillo’s practice has been concerned with the simplicity of the line. “As simple as they were, they were the most complex because it’s hard to get to simplicity right away,” she once told ARTnews about her line drawings. For her latest solo show, titled “Pause in Time,” Jaramillo will present new entries into two longstanding bodies of works: her “Curvilinear” series, in which two bending lines stretch across a monochrome canvas, and linen-fiber works, rough-hewn collages of cut and torn fragments of a medium of Jaramillo’s own making (water, linen-fiber pulp, and hand-ground earth pigments). Both are stylistic approaches that she has revisited again and again in her practice, adding a new level of understanding between her well-known highly formal works and the materiality of her collage pieces. 547 West 20th Street, November 12–December 18

Mildred Thompson at Galerie Lelong Image Credit: ©The Mildred Thompson Estate/Courtesy Galerie Lelong “Cosmos Calling” presents four 1996 paintings from Mildred Thompson’s “Music of the Spheres” series alongside three from her “Heliocentric Series,” made a few years earlier. In the earlier works, we see Thompson approaching the organization of the solar system, via spinning lines that mark planetary movements, in vertical canvases. When she homes in on individual planets—Mercury, Venus, Mars, and Jupiter here— the canvases are turned horizontally, and her use of color becomes kinetic and eye-popping. “I seek to portray some of the profound meanings and influences indicated by the invisible dimensions and realities around us,” Thompson once said of these works. In doing so, she makes tangible the intangible, revealing forces just beyond our physical and intellectual grasp. 528 West 26th Street, through December 19

Norman Lewis at Michael Rosenfeld Gallery Image Credit: ©Estate of Norman Lewis/Courtesy Michael Rosenfeld Gallery LLC, New York For its seventh exhibition of the late and great Norman Lewis, Michael Rosenfeld Gallery has on view “Jumping Jive,” which looks at the influence of music, from jazz to classical to reggae, across the artist’s four-decade career. Surprisingly, the exhibition includes two of Lewis’s early figurative works, Jumping Jive (1942) and Musicians (1943). Chronologically, the next work, an untitled canvas from ca. 1945, shows how Lewis began to translate the sonic into paint, taking inspiration from the intuitive and improvisational nature of jazz. As the 1940s progress into the ’50s and ’60s, we see how Lewis’s work became even more abstracted, often suspending various marks across deep color fields. The paintings on view are complemented by several works on paper that give further insight into the artist’s way of working. The back of the gallery also includes a DJ booth, displaying Lewis’s record collection. Each Saturday, from 2–5 p.m., DJ Adrian will spin these vinyls; a recording of the session will play in the gallery for the following week. 100 11th Avenue, through November 14

Mary Lovelace O’Neal at Boesky Gallery Image Credit: ©Mary Lovelace O'Neal/Courtesy Boesky Gallery The first solo exhibition since Mary Lovelace O’Neal’s death in May, “Requiem” will present historical works by the artist. Made between the 1980s and ’90s, the paintings on view in this show look at the period immediately following Lovelace O’Neal’s relocation to the Bay Area in the late ’70s. Her formalist Minimal paintings of that decade give way to a much more expressive use of mark-making and a vibrant color palette. In the works on view, limbs and other familiar forms and figures seem to emerge from the depths of the built-up paint, part of the artist’s subversion of the typical rules of abstraction. The titles she gives to these works— Juke Joint , Panthers with Socks , or What’s time to a pig , for example—further complicate their readings. 507 West 24th Street, through December 19

Dia al-Azzawi at Richard Saltoun Gallery Image Credit: ©Dia Al-Azzawi/Courtesy Richard Saltoun Gallery, London, Rome, and New York Following an exhibition this spring at Richard Saltoun Gallery’s homebase in London, Dia al-Azzawi will have his first-ever gallery solo show in New York and the first since his memorable inclusions in “Theater of Operations: The Gulf Wars 1991–2011” at MoMA PS1 (2019–20) and “Taking Shape: Abstraction from The Arab World, 1950s–1980s” at the Grey Art Gallery (2020). Born in Baghdad in 1939 and based in London since 1976, al-Azzawi is known for his abstract works that typically make use of Arabic script in their compositions. Titled “Tell Us a Tale to Break the Waking Night,” the exhibition brings together works from across his career, ranging from Arabic Letters (1970) to Man in Yellow Field (2020–21). 19 East 66th Street, through December 19

Alejandro Corujeira at Hutchinson Modern & Contemporary Image Credit: Courtesy Hutchinson Modern & Contemporary For his second solo show with Hutchinson Modern & Contemporary, Alejandro Corujeira is showing 11 paintings made over the last three years. Of his way of working, he has said, “I am not slow. I am delayed.” With a muted color palette of turquoises, coppers, and yellows, Corujeira continues his investigations into the properties of light and how to make them visible, as indicated by the exhibition’s title “La Sonora Luz de lo Invisible” (Sounding Light of the Unseen). The works’ titles give a clue to these ponderings, too: La levedad de la luz (The lightness of light) or El viento en la luz (The wind of the light). Lines and blobs vibrate until fuzzy, achieved via a mix of colored pencil and acrylic on linen. 47 East 64th Street, through January 30

Nairy Baghramian at Marian Goodman Gallery Image Credit: Courtesy the artist and Marian Goodman Gallery The only sculptor included in the mix, Nairy Baghramian will show a range of recent works at Marian Goodman Gallery, including examples from her “nameless” series, made of neon tubes, glass, aluminum, and silicon, that debuted last year in her solo show at WIELS in Belgium. These will be paired with works from her “oreiller” series, nearly translucent sculptures made of epoxy resin, wood, and metal, and her “selves” series, abstract works made from applying layers of pigmented wax onto oiled maple. Taken together, the works on view present various ways of thinking about paradoxes, a hallmark of Baghramian’s work: What does it mean to name something “nameless”? Can a self-portrait be a relief of built-up pigment? As Baghramian has said, “What draws me to neon is its tendency to flicker, as though its eternal promise were already showing signs of fatigue.” 385 Broadway, November 11–January 16

"早在新浪潮出現之前的1970年代初，香港電影已經歷了連番影響深遠的變化，包括粵語片的消亡與再生，嘉禾的興起，獨立製片的活躍等。還有一個大轉變是一些舊類型的消退與及功夫片、黑幫片和警匪片等新類型的出現。這個年代已不再是明星一紅便甚麼類型都能演能賣座的時期。每個類型都有屬於它的明星。剛去世的陳觀泰便是屬於類型的明星。但比較特別的，是他自成名便已同時立足於兩個重要的新類型——功夫片和黑幫片——之上。 眾所周知，陳觀泰因主演張徹執導的《馬永貞》（1972）一炮而紅，成為張徹的「契仔」。張徹是當時最能發掘男明星和最有策略捧新人的一位導演。行內把他捧紅的男星稱之為他的「契仔」。在陳之前，張已捧紅了第一代契仔王羽、羅烈和第二代契仔姜大衞、狄龍。他在《馬永貞》中要捧陳觀泰，便用已大紅的姜大衞演譚四一角，與陳觀泰演的馬永貞打一場平手的架然後惺惺相惜起來，抬高陳作為明星的地位。《馬》片票房二百多萬，刷新了張徹電影的賣座紀錄。陳遂成為繼姜大衞、狄龍之後紅起來的第二代契仔。三人有時會以三人組方式聯合演出，例如《年輕人》（1972）和《刺馬》（1973），也繼續帶新人，加進王鍾合演了《四騎士》（1972），然後四人加進李修賢合演《五虎將》（1974），一個帶一個。張徹離開邵氏搞自己的公司長弓，起初仍在香港拍戲。陳觀泰照樣為他帶新星，在《方世玉與洪熙官》（1974）中帶傅聲，《少林子弟》（1974）則二人一起帶戚冠軍。長弓移師台灣，陳觀泰留在邵氏沒有跟隨。但與張徹維持良好關係，張徹後來回邵氏依然有找他演出。1980年代兩度攝製張徹紀念作《上海灘十三太保》（1984）和《義膽群英》（1989）他都有參演。陳觀泰的成名實有賴張徹的眼光和栽培，而他對張也一直報以情義。 《馬永貞》 雖說陳在《馬永貞》一炮而紅，但在演《馬永貞》之前他已在影圈浮沉了一陣子。陳本身習武，是大聖劈掛門弟子，師從陳秀中。在兼受了一段日子的西洋拳訓練後，於1969參加第一屆東南亞國術邀請賽，獲得輕量級甲組冠軍。但這樣強的搏擊背景對他從影幫助不大，只能任配角和武師。他在粵語片《學府新潮》（1970）演欺負鄧光榮的飛仔同學，在《黃飛鴻勇破烈火陣》（1970）中演凌雲楷，角色雖有點份量，但他並未惹來關注。他也曾隨資深的陳少鵬一起在楚原執導的《龍沐香》（1970）任武指，但他參與國語片時大都只是任武師，行就行先，死就死先。直到《唐山大兄》（1971）極度賣座，香港電影發生翻天覆地的大變，影圈急切找尋打得之人作新星。陳觀泰擂台上的輝煌歷史頓然奇貨可居，被張徹相中，主演了拳腳打鬥電影《馬永貞》。在影片中他除了連番以寡敵眾所向披靡，還特意讓他在擂台上打敗洋人——當時在香港知名的澳洲摔角手「君子」馬蘭奴，建立陳擁有真功夫的形象。從這個角度看，陳可說是邵氏第一位功夫明星。陳的外貌不如姜大衞、狄龍英俊，但他有着沉實厚重的形象，與姜、狄又自不同。這不得不說張徹眼光的獨到，他捧的男星儘管同樣具備男性的陽剛魅力，每個男星又各有自己的個性和魅力。 陳觀泰以搏擊冠軍頭銜建立的真功夫形象，最適合往功夫片方面發展。張徹自立長弓，嘗試以「少林功夫片」作為公司路線，首作《方世玉與洪熙官》便由已成名的陳觀泰演洪熙官，帶領傅聲出道，由傅演方世玉。張徹想出一個方法來強調影片的真功夫感覺——片頭加映一個以天幕為背景，由陳觀泰、傅聲、戚冠軍演式的短片《洪拳三路》。由於他們耍得拳風虎虎，觀眾遂相信他們是好打之人。這個做法很可能學自盲俠片，經張使用後，成為後來無數功夫片的開場模式，包括劉家良的《陸阿采與黃飛鴻》（1976）、成龍的《蛇形刁手》（1978）等。《方》片說清廷火燒少林寺後，少林門徒方世玉不知洪熙官是同門，誤會他是壞人害他遭清兵所捕。方知道真相後努力救他。編劇倪匡大概借用了《書劍恩仇錄》前段紅花會救奔雷手文泰的劇情，洪熙官就像文泰來一樣，主要劇情都是被捕受困。兩個主角的性格，方世玉似鶴，英氣逼人如鶴立雞群。洪熙官似虎，縱然虎落平陽，依然有王者氣派，一旦縱虎歸山，就大發虎威。二人最後聯手以虎鶴雙形拳擊殺大反派朱牧。陳觀泰為洪熙官注入了大度質樸的氣質，成為以後影視處理洪熙官的基礎。後來劉家良拍功夫片，在《陸阿采與黃飛鴻》找陳觀泰演黃飛鴻的師祖陸阿采，借陳的功夫片地位來捧主角劉家輝，一樣成功。之後更以陳任主角演出《洪熙官》（1977）。劉當年是《方世玉與洪熙》的武指，自己任導演拍《洪熙官》，少了張徹的血腥，但動作更精緻流麗。戲中洪熙官使的是虎形拳。招式打來威猛剛勁，配合角色性格的剛毅木訥，最適合陳發揮。洪為破大敵白眉的金鐘罩，要苦練在彈珠銅人身上取珠的練功戲，畫面與音效都非常吸引。倪匡的劇本描述洪熙官起初打不過就跑，回去苦練期望下次能打贏。但到虎形拳練到登峰造極之後，即使打敗不逃寧願戰死，因為知道自己的極限，那種大丈夫在可逃不可逃的分際掌握得十分準確，其最後的死也就特別悲壯。《洪熙官》是陳觀泰功夫片中的代表作。陳的功夫片還有一部值得一記，他曾為獨立公司自導自演《鐵馬騮》（1977），主角在少林學藝，從猴子身上參悟出猴拳，那自是一次向對師門的回饋。 《方世玉與洪熙官》 武俠明星不一定能演功夫片，但功夫片明星兼演武俠片則無礙觀眾接受。陳觀泰在邵氏主演過兩部很重要的武俠片。第一部是何夢華的《血滴子》（1975）。血滴子早在民國武俠小說已出現，在之前的武俠片也偶爾會見過，但看着它蓋着人頭把頭切掉，血從沒有頭臚的頸項中狂噴的震撼畫面，應始自邵氏的這部《血滴子》。影片賣座，不單邵氏自己拍了兩部續集，港台也出現一些跟風作，「血滴子」才紅到國外。陳第二部重要武俠片是桂治洪的《萬人斬》（1980）。影片重拍張徹的《鐵手無情》，陳觀泰演捕頭冷天鷹，領着部下去緝捕盜去大內金庫金子的匪幫，不斷遭遇頑抗。陳使的刀刀身長而闊，不時要用雙手使，打法別具特色。桂治洪很重視環境和氣氛，最後大雨中的泥濘爛戰更是大異一般武俠片。陳演冷天鷹亦入形入格。以金庸角色來模擬選角，他適合演文泰來（可惜楚原為邵氏拍《書劍》沒有用他），《神鵰》郭靖（在《楊過與小龍女》中確實演過），外形也可演喬峰，但演技不足以演到喬峰個性和感情的複雜。 談完陳演出的功夫片武俠片，跟着談他演的黑幫片，這卻要回到原點由《馬永貞》說起。當年由於賣的是陳的真功夫，《馬永貞》自然被觀眾歸入功夫片。但是我在《無惡不作——香港黑幫片的肌理脈絡》一書中已指出，從類型角度分析，它實在是部黑幫片。馬永貞是由鄉下到大城市的小人物，憑着膽色和勇力在黑道上成為一方之霸，這完全是美國經典黑幫片的戲劇程式，我稱之為「大佬黑幫片」。《馬永貞》是香港黑幫片的濫觴。張徹其後拍出《馬》的續集《仇連環》（1972），陳觀泰依然有着打出頭的性格，只是造型改為穿着有型的皮褸。陳跟着演了桂治洪的《成記茶樓》（1974）。《成記茶樓》改編自江之南的小說《人在江湖》，陳飾演的大哥成在小說中是個黑道中人，但在電影中已改為有義氣只是裝黑道的茶樓老闆，帶着夥計自行執法除暴安良。《成記茶樓》不能算作正式的黑幫片，但也延續了陳觀泰在《馬永貞》建立的大佬形象。《成》片由於賣座，邵氏出品了續集《大哥成》（1975）及衍生影片《沙膽英》（1976），都是由陳觀泰演大哥成。也就因了黑幫大佬的形象，他主演了麗的黑幫劇《人在江湖》（1980），飾演販毒起家的毒梟石家威。與他黑幫大佬形象相關的，1970年代中他也開始演反派。特別重要的是在程剛執導的《賭王大騙局》（1976）中演大反派「牌霸」彭天石，是主角沙家要打倒的大敵。《賭》片賣座近一百五十萬，票房排在該年邵氏出品的前五名內。它是香港賭千片的開山之作，之後不少續作仿作，包括王晶創作的電視劇《千王之王》（1980）和《千王群英會》（1981）。到王晶挾電視上的成功進邵氏，首作《千王鬥千霸》（1981）便依然是賭千片，演「千王」的是《千王之王》的謝賢，反派「千霸」則是《賭王大騙局》的陳觀泰。王再為邵氏拍《賊王之王》，演「賊王」謝賢對手的依然是陳觀泰。正如「牌霸」「千霸」的角色名字，陳觀泰演的反派多是惡霸型，擁有龐大勢力行出來有威勢。他與另一位也是由主角轉做反派的岳華是很好的對比。岳華演技強，專能演似忠實奸的雙面人，陳觀泰氣場較強，適合演惡霸型的反派。繼續以金庸人物作模擬選角，岳華適合演岳不群，而陳觀泰適合演左冷禪。 《成記茶樓》 陳觀泰是屬於1970年代的。1980年之後，他雖然仍有演出電影電視，但已沒有甚麼突破性發展。他的硬橋硬馬功夫，在成龍、洪金寶等雜耍式動作興起後便因缺乏靈巧而不合時宜。陳的限制在他雖然擁有鮮明的明星形象，但演技沒有提升，沒辦法把自己的演出領域擴闊。好像演惡霸型反派，同類角色演過一兩次便會因缺乏變化而顯得乏味。但放在1970年代，他同時是功夫片和黑幫片兩個類型具代表性的明星，留下了《馬永貞》、《成記茶樓》、《洪熙官》和《萬人斬》等佳作，實足以自豪。 陳在1980年之後雖沒大發展，但仍有一些演出值得一記。陳在1980年代演出過不少台灣電影電視劇。曾夥拍楊惠珊合演抗戰背景的女性復仇片《浪女神龍劍》（1982）。台灣四個最有名的鬼故事，他主演了其中兩個，包括改編「呂祖廟燒金」的《屠夫》（1984）和《周成過台灣》（1988）。《周成過台灣》把一個負心漢故事改成渡台男人的困境，頗適合他質樸的氣質。他和周星馳合演過《小偷阿星》（1990），演一個失憶臥底，幸遇周演的小偷幫他重拾記憶。陳演來毫無喜劇感。同是1970年代打仔出身，與周星馳合作的喜劇效果，陳既比不上梁家仁，比《風雨同路》（1990）中的陳惠敏也尚有不如。 《打擂台》 陳觀泰晚年仍有一些重要的演出。最重要的一次是與同在今年去世的梁小龍主演了《打擂台》（2010）。《打》片滿是香港武打片的情懷，有不少過去武打片的演員參與，對陳、梁二人的打星歷史尤其顯出尊重。陳出場時是只求息事寧人的鄉村茶樓老闆，但發展下去是老而彌堅的武功好手。影片尾段讓他與羅莽漂亮地打了一場，來強調他的寶刀未老，對他的打仔身份致以崇高的敬意。陳之後還演過王晶監製黃精甫執導的《惡戰》（2014），《惡戰》是新版本的馬永貞，演馬永貞的是伍允龍。影片知道找陳觀泰參與有意思，卻又叫他演一個沒有份量的小角色，地位幾乎變回他未成名前的武師，我看時竟有點為他感到悲哀。反而在徐皓峰的《師父》（2015）中，他出場機會也不多，但卻有着特別的地位。影片結局是由廖凡演的詠春傳人以雙刀挑盡天津兵器好手逃亡，陳觀泰演壓軸最後一位出手的元老。由是見到香港以外，陳的打星地位也同樣受到徐皓峰這位中國優秀武打導演的尊重，值得欣慰。"}]

雖說陳在《馬永貞》一炮而紅，但在演《馬永貞》之前他已在影圈浮沉了一陣子。陳本身習武，是大聖劈掛門弟子，師從陳秀中。在兼受了一段日子的西洋拳訓練後，於1969參加第一屆東南亞國術邀請賽，獲得輕量級甲組冠軍。但這樣強的搏擊背景對他從影幫助不大，只能任配角和武師。他在粵語片《學府新潮》（1970）演欺負鄧光榮的飛仔同學，在《黃飛鴻勇破烈火陣》（1970）中演凌雲楷，角色雖有點份量，但他並未惹來關注。他也曾隨資深的陳少鵬一起在楚原執導的《龍沐香》（1970）任武指，但他參與國語片時大都只是任武師，行就行先，死就死先。直到《唐山大兄》（1971）極度賣座，香港電影發生翻天覆地的大變，影圈急切找尋打得之人作新星。陳觀泰擂台上的輝煌歷史頓然奇貨可居，被張徹相中，主演了拳腳打鬥電影《馬永貞》。在影片中他除了連番以寡敵眾所向披靡，還特意讓他在擂台上打敗洋人——當時在香港知名的澳洲摔角手「君子」馬蘭奴，建立陳擁有真功夫的形象。從這個角度看，陳可說是邵氏第一位功夫明星。陳的外貌不如姜大衞、狄龍英俊，但他有着沉實厚重的形象，與姜、狄又自不同。這不得不說張徹眼光的獨到，他捧的男星儘管同樣具備男性的陽剛魅力，每個男星又各有自己的個性和魅力。 陳觀泰以搏擊冠軍頭銜建立的真功夫形象，最適合往功夫片方面發展。張徹自立長弓，嘗試以「少林功夫片」作為公司路線，首作《方世玉與洪熙官》便由已成名的陳觀泰演洪熙官，帶領傅聲出道，由傅演方世玉。張徹想出一個方法來強調影片的真功夫感覺——片頭加映一個以天幕為背景，由陳觀泰、傅聲、戚冠軍演式的短片《洪拳三路》。由於他們耍得拳風虎虎，觀眾遂相信他們是好打之人。這個做法很可能學自盲俠片，經張使用後，成為後來無數功夫片的開場模式，包括劉家良的《陸阿采與黃飛鴻》（1976）、成龍的《蛇形刁手》（1978）等。《方》片說清廷火燒少林寺後，少林門徒方世玉不知洪熙官是同門，誤會他是壞人害他遭清兵所捕。方知道真相後努力救他。編劇倪匡大概借用了《書劍恩仇錄》前段紅花會救奔雷手文泰的劇情，洪熙官就像文泰來一樣，主要劇情都是被捕受困。兩個主角的性格，方世玉似鶴，英氣逼人如鶴立雞群。洪熙官似虎，縱然虎落平陽，依然有王者氣派，一旦縱虎歸山，就大發虎威。二人最後聯手以虎鶴雙形拳擊殺大反派朱牧。陳觀泰為洪熙官注入了大度質樸的氣質，成為以後影視處理洪熙官的基礎。後來劉家良拍功夫片，在《陸阿采與黃飛鴻》找陳觀泰演黃飛鴻的師祖陸阿采，借陳的功夫片地位來捧主角劉家輝，一樣成功。之後更以陳任主角演出《洪熙官》（1977）。劉當年是《方世玉與洪熙》的武指，自己任導演拍《洪熙官》，少了張徹的血腥，但動作更精緻流麗。戲中洪熙官使的是虎形拳。招式打來威猛剛勁，配合角色性格的剛毅木訥，最適合陳發揮。洪為破大敵白眉的金鐘罩，要苦練在彈珠銅人身上取珠的練功戲，畫面與音效都非常吸引。倪匡的劇本描述洪熙官起初打不過就跑，回去苦練期望下次能打贏。但到虎形拳練到登峰造極之後，即使打敗不逃寧願戰死，因為知道自己的極限，那種大丈夫在可逃不可逃的分際掌握得十分準確，其最後的死也就特別悲壯。《洪熙官》是陳觀泰功夫片中的代表作。陳的功夫片還有一部值得一記，他曾為獨立公司自導自演《鐵馬騮》（1977），主角在少林學藝，從猴子身上參悟出猴拳，那自是一次向對師門的回饋。 《方世玉與洪熙官》 武俠明星不一定能演功夫片，但功夫片明星兼演武俠片則無礙觀眾接受。陳觀泰在邵氏主演過兩部很重要的武俠片。第一部是何夢華的《血滴子》（1975）。血滴子早在民國武俠小說已出現，在之前的武俠片也偶爾會見過，但看着它蓋着人頭把頭切掉，血從沒有頭臚的頸項中狂噴的震撼畫面，應始自邵氏的這部《血滴子》。影片賣座，不單邵氏自己拍了兩部續集，港台也出現一些跟風作，「血滴子」才紅到國外。陳第二部重要武俠片是桂治洪的《萬人斬》（1980）。影片重拍張徹的《鐵手無情》，陳觀泰演捕頭冷天鷹，領着部下去緝捕盜去大內金庫金子的匪幫，不斷遭遇頑抗。陳使的刀刀身長而闊，不時要用雙手使，打法別具特色。桂治洪很重視環境和氣氛，最後大雨中的泥濘爛戰更是大異一般武俠片。陳演冷天鷹亦入形入格。以金庸角色來模擬選角，他適合演文泰來（可惜楚原為邵氏拍《書劍》沒有用他），《神鵰》郭靖（在《楊過與小龍女》中確實演過），外形也可演喬峰，但演技不足以演到喬峰個性和感情的複雜。 談完陳演出的功夫片武俠片，跟着談他演的黑幫片，這卻要回到原點由《馬永貞》說起。當年由於賣的是陳的真功夫，《馬永貞》自然被觀眾歸入功夫片。但是我在《無惡不作——香港黑幫片的肌理脈絡》一書中已指出，從類型角度分析，它實在是部黑幫片。馬永貞是由鄉下到大城市的小人物，憑着膽色和勇力在黑道上成為一方之霸，這完全是美國經典黑幫片的戲劇程式，我稱之為「大佬黑幫片」。《馬永貞》是香港黑幫片的濫觴。張徹其後拍出《馬》的續集《仇連環》（1972），陳觀泰依然有着打出頭的性格，只是造型改為穿着有型的皮褸。陳跟着演了桂治洪的《成記茶樓》（1974）。《成記茶樓》改編自江之南的小說《人在江湖》，陳飾演的大哥成在小說中是個黑道中人，但在電影中已改為有義氣只是裝黑道的茶樓老闆，帶着夥計自行執法除暴安良。《成記茶樓》不能算作正式的黑幫片，但也延續了陳觀泰在《馬永貞》建立的大佬形象。《成》片由於賣座，邵氏出品了續集《大哥成》（1975）及衍生影片《沙膽英》（1976），都是由陳觀泰演大哥成。也就因了黑幫大佬的形象，他主演了麗的黑幫劇《人在江湖》（1980），飾演販毒起家的毒梟石家威。與他黑幫大佬形象相關的，1970年代中他也開始演反派。特別重要的是在程剛執導的《賭王大騙局》（1976）中演大反派「牌霸」彭天石，是主角沙家要打倒的大敵。《賭》片賣座近一百五十萬，票房排在該年邵氏出品的前五名內。它是香港賭千片的開山之作，之後不少續作仿作，包括王晶創作的電視劇《千王之王》（1980）和《千王群英會》（1981）。到王晶挾電視上的成功進邵氏，首作《千王鬥千霸》（1981）便依然是賭千片，演「千王」的是《千王之王》的謝賢，反派「千霸」則是《賭王大騙局》的陳觀泰。王再為邵氏拍《賊王之王》，演「賊王」謝賢對手的依然是陳觀泰。正如「牌霸」「千霸」的角色名字，陳觀泰演的反派多是惡霸型，擁有龐大勢力行出來有威勢。他與另一位也是由主角轉做反派的岳華是很好的對比。岳華演技強，專能演似忠實奸的雙面人，陳觀泰氣場較強，適合演惡霸型的反派。繼續以金庸人物作模擬選角，岳華適合演岳不群，而陳觀泰適合演左冷禪。 《成記茶樓》 陳觀泰是屬於1970年代的。1980年之後，他雖然仍有演出電影電視，但已沒有甚麼突破性發展。他的硬橋硬馬功夫，在成龍、洪金寶等雜耍式動作興起後便因缺乏靈巧而不合時宜。陳的限制在他雖然擁有鮮明的明星形象，但演技沒有提升，沒辦法把自己的演出領域擴闊。好像演惡霸型反派，同類角色演過一兩次便會因缺乏變化而顯得乏味。但放在1970年代，他同時是功夫片和黑幫片兩個類型具代表性的明星，留下了《馬永貞》、《成記茶樓》、《洪熙官》和《萬人斬》等佳作，實足以自豪。 陳在1980年之後雖沒大發展，但仍有一些演出值得一記。陳在1980年代演出過不少台灣電影電視劇。曾夥拍楊惠珊合演抗戰背景的女性復仇片《浪女神龍劍》（1982）。台灣四個最有名的鬼故事，他主演了其中兩個，包括改編「呂祖廟燒金」的《屠夫》（1984）和《周成過台灣》（1988）。《周成過台灣》把一個負心漢故事改成渡台男人的困境，頗適合他質樸的氣質。他和周星馳合演過《小偷阿星》（1990），演一個失憶臥底，幸遇周演的小偷幫他重拾記憶。陳演來毫無喜劇感。同是1970年代打仔出身，與周星馳合作的喜劇效果，陳既比不上梁家仁，比《風雨同路》（1990）中的陳惠敏也尚有不如。 《打擂台》 陳觀泰晚年仍有一些重要的演出。最重要的一次是與同在今年去世的梁小龍主演了《打擂台》（2010）。《打》片滿是香港武打片的情懷，有不少過去武打片的演員參與，對陳、梁二人的打星歷史尤其顯出尊重。陳出場時是只求息事寧人的鄉村茶樓老闆，但發展下去是老而彌堅的武功好手。影片尾段讓他與羅莽漂亮地打了一場，來強調他的寶刀未老，對他的打仔身份致以崇高的敬意。陳之後還演過王晶監製黃精甫執導的《惡戰》（2014），《惡戰》是新版本的馬永貞，演馬永貞的是伍允龍。影片知道找陳觀泰參與有意思，卻又叫他演一個沒有份量的小角色，地位幾乎變回他未成名前的武師，我看時竟有點為他感到悲哀。反而在徐皓峰的《師父》（2015）中，他出場機會也不多，但卻有着特別的地位。影片結局是由廖凡演的詠春傳人以雙刀挑盡天津兵器好手逃亡，陳觀泰演壓軸最後一位出手的元老。由是見到香港以外，陳的打星地位也同樣受到徐皓峰這位中國優秀武打導演的尊重，值得欣慰。
