article_text:
Comic book writer and screenwriter Frank Miller – whose work includes “300,” “Sin City” and “Batman: The Dark Knight Returns” – returned this week to Lucca Comics and Games , an event that spans the gamut of geek culture and pop entertainment.

As well as speaking at the event, to coincide with the 40th anniversary of “Batman: The Dark Knight Returns,” Miller also introduced “Frank Miller – American Genius,” Silenn Thomas’ documentary about his impact on popular culture.

Related Stories

Netflix Content Chief Bela Bajaria on Overseeing Global Storytelling: 'My Super Power Is I Hire Really Great People and I Let Them Do Their Job'

‘The New Stanford Prison Experiment’ Creators Break Down Its Shocking Finale

Variety spoke to Miller about politics, art and why he’s relieved there are fewer comic book movies this year.

Would you agree that there has been a slight dip in the comic book to movie pipeline? I would hope so. Yeah, really. It had really gotten so out of control that comics had started losing much of their own identity. I have been arguing vehemently for comics to start asserting their own purpose again and asserting their own identity as a literary form.

Do you think there were too many comic book artists and writers aiming for movie and TV deals? Oh, without question. Just because the appeal of not just the money, but the fame, respect and glory of working in the most powerful medium in history is undeniable, but I think that it was a little too heady a wine, in that comics were really in danger of losing their souls in the process.

It very much seemed to be superhero movies in particular. Oh, that was all it was. It was partly because the technology caught up with us. So the one thing comics could do that nobody else could do was the ridiculous pyrotechnics and everything, right? But if you think of it, the die was cast back in the 1970s with the movie slogan “You’ll believe a man can fly” where they actually made Superman’s flight convincing, and now they can do, you know, virtually anything that can be imagined.

Some of your finest work has been inspired by cinema, but has not necessarily involved superheroes: “Sin City” and “300” for instance. Well, yes, my entire oeuvre has been dedicated to defining and redefining the hero, and sometimes making him as ugly as possible, as in Marv and “Sin City,” and other times torturing the hero: as with Hartigan in the “Sin City: That Yellow Bastard” story. The exploration of the hero is just infinitely fascinating. Once you let go of the idea of the hero being society’s voice, it becomes more an examination of the human spirit.

As well as the heroes, you create astonishing, extreme worlds. But it seems that we live in a world which is almost impossible to exaggerate. I often have remarked that doing the next “Martha Washington” would be difficult because the first one happened. And my parody of Ronald Reagan is now in the White House, right? But there’s always somewhere else to go. Now you would parody what my country has turned into, and what the world has turned into, it’s fascinating dark material, indeed.

It’s almost like Dante looking at hell and going, “I see some verses here.” There’s no shortage of inspiration now. This is indeed a supercharged time, because in the course of the 20th century, there were two gigantic realignments, through the two world wars, particularly World War II, which was a gigantic, unifying event. World War II was the advent of American hegemony, but now we’re at the other side of the American hegemony. America has become much like Rome: spread so far and so rich and powerful that it has lost its center. It is no longer Thomas Jefferson’s country, for instance. It is no longer the land of the free and the home of the brave. It’s become quite a bloated thing, and of course this is exactly when we start waving the flag more than ever, right?

When I see the MAGA signs I ask whether by saying “again,” you are saying that it’s not great. There are so many contradictions within all of that, but this is a global situation. The old order is, as Bob Dylan put it, rapidly aging, and so everywhere you look, there’s an empire crumbling. Look at the thrashing old Soviet Union, right? And what it’s dissolving into, when a tiny brave country is bringing it to its knees. China has become a paranoid concentration camp. So we’re definitely seeing a change in the matrix. Speaking of the Chinese, this does bring to mind the old curse: May you live in interesting times. We live in interesting times, don’t we?

Watching the documentary “American Genius” I noticed you didn’t seem to listen to music when you work. I’ll either work and just have the street sounds, or I’ll have NPR on, listening to world news. That’s helpful to me, especially when I’m drawing. It helps me remove one sphere of my mind from play to a certain extent, and to let the verbal side of my mind be occupied, and let the freer, more relaxed, visually-oriented side take over because most of the drawing work is the actual clinical, decisive part of the illustration. I work that out on a sheet of tracing paper, and then when it comes to executing the drawing, I want to be as relaxed as possible and not be consciously thinking too much, revealing more. So if I’m drawing someone who’s angry, for instance, I’m striking the face with brush strokes that are angry ones. It gets into a more jazz rhythm. Whereas when I’m plotting a story or when I’m writing dialog that is verbal work. So I want to be focusing more on that side of my mind.

What next? Well, I’m working with the great Italian artist Milo Manara, who is renowned for his erotic and often funny comic book work. He asked me on stage once if I would write a “Sin City” story for him. He’s the only artist I could ever imagine doing one with, because I’ve always drawn them all myself. But this is the one exception I’ll make because … I told him on stage, being glib: Yes, I’ll do it but he’d have to learn how to draw women.

[Miller also announced during his stay at Lucca that he would be collaborating once more with Japanese artist Peach Momoko with whom he’d previously worked on “Tears of the Spider Queen” for Marvel.]

article_text:
Trine Dyrholm , Christian Slater , Dree Hemingway are set to star in Jesper Just ’s Incidents of Intimacy , the second production in Zentropa ’s new collection of Dogma25 pictures.

The initiative rebooting the Danish company’s 1995 Dogma Manifesto was first announced during the Cannes Film Festival last May.

Dyrholm will star as a woman who is unable to acknowledge and access her own feelings and constructs intimacy by stealing objects from people instead of getting close to them. After having emotional reactions through the objects, she files them in an archive of intimacy in her cupboard.

Related Stories

Dogma 25: Isabella Eklöf Among Group Of Scandi Filmmakers Launching Refreshed Manifesto

‘Nobody Wants This’ Creator Erin Foster Has “More Story To Tell” With A Season 4, But Isn’t Getting “Too Attached”

When a triangular relationship appears, it destabilizes her system, causing emotions to detach from their origins and circulate independently. Gradually, the objects take on a life of their own and the control she’s been holding on to slips through her fingers. Her controlled world is turned into a site of emotional horror as a new reality dawns, created and dominated by autonomous feelings.

Watch on Deadline

Danish actors Johannes Lilleøre ( Unit One ), Julie Agnete Vang ( The Commune ), Laura Drasbæk ( The Killing ) and Michael Moritzen ( The Legacy ) are also in the cast.

Dyrholm’s casting in Incidents of Intimacy marks a homecoming for the Danish actress who was part of the ensemble cast in Thomas Vinterberg’s Cannes Jury Prize winner The Celebration , the first film to be made under the original manifesto.

Now one of Denmark ’s best known actresses, her credits since include Susanne Bier’s Academy Award-winning drama In A Better World , Nikolaj Arcel’s A Royal Affair, May el-Toukhy ’s Queen of Hearts and in recent years in Magnus von Horn’s The Girl With The Needle and Jeanette Nordahl’s Beginnings.

Dyrholm will star opposite The Name of the Rose break out and Mr. Robot Golden Globe winning star Slater, who also has Zentropa connections having appeared in a supporting role in Lars von Trier’s 2013 erotic drama Nymphomaniac . Hemingway is known for her roles in Sean Baker’s S tarlet , FX limited series Love Story and While We’re Young .

Incidents of Intimacy is the first feature film of Just, an acclaimed artist whose work has been shown worldwide and can be found in the collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, Guggenheim Museum, Tate Modern and Helsinki’s Museum of Contemporary Art Kiasma among many more.

He has just completed the script in collaboration with Sissel Dalsgaard Thomsen, who was also the script writer behind Isabella Eklöf’s Kalak and Malene Choi’s The Quiet Migration .

Dogma25 is an initiative of recent Venice Golden Lion winner May el-Toukhy ( Woman Unknown) , who will be one of the five directors making films under its rules alongside directors Milad Alami, Annika Berg, Eklöf and Just.

The five filmmakers have united in an artistic collective based on a shared manifesto and a new vow of chastity comprising ten new dogmas [check them out below] to protect the artistic integrity of feature film and create space for uncompromising cinematic storytelling. All five feature films will be produced by Zentropa.

The Danish Dogma25 projects are financed in a collaboration between Zentropa, DR, and Nordisk Film Distribution, with the addition of Netflix in the Nordics, constituting the core financing necessary to realize all five projects.

Additionally, Incidents of Intimacy is produced with support from the Danish Film Institute, The Eastern Denmark Film Fund and Nordisk Film & TV Fond.

The Dogma25 films are distributed by Nordisk Film Distribution and subsequently on Netflix in the Nordics and DR. TrustNordisk handles international sales.

The Rules of the Dogma25 ‘Vow of Chastity’

1. The script must be original and handwritten by the director. We compel ourselves to write the script by hand in order to nurture the kind of intuition that flows most freely from the dream, channelled through the hand onto the paper.

2. At least half the film must be without dialogue. We insist on a cinematic approach to filmmaking, because we believe in visual storytelling and have faith in the audience.

3. The internet is off limits in all creative processes. We commit to produce the films relying on real people within our physical reality – rather than in a digital one infused with algorithms.

4. We’ll only accept funding with no content altering conditions attached. We assume responsibility for keeping budgets down so the team retains final say in all artistic decisions.

5. No more than 10 people behind the camera. We commit to working in close collaborations to build trust and strengthen our shared vision.

6. The film must be shot where the narrative takes place. Film as an art form becomes artificial and generic when we portray a location in a false light.

7. We’re not allowed to use make-up or manipulate faces and bodies unless it’s part of the narrative. Just as we strive to maintain the authenticity of the location, we also want to portray the human body without a filter. We celebrate it – warts and all.

8. Everything relating to the film’s production must be rented, borrowed, found, or used. We commit to making films using objects that already exist and renounce the ahistorical and self-destructive culture of consumerism.

9. The film must be made in no more than one year. We abstain from any lengthy processes that stand in the way of creative flow.

10. Create the film as if it were your last.
